intervals.note: Month precision. Their first run lasted five consecutive days; they returned on 29 August and ran until the Bevatron broke down on 5 September. The end is the publication-date bound of the completed interval.
intervals.quote: The antiproton experiments of the Segrè and Chamberlain team began the first week of August 1955.

intervals.note: A bound, not an end-of-run date: the discovery run documented here was over by the date of the Physical Review paper. Later antiproton work at the Bevatron is outside this record.

name: Bevatron antiproton experiment
notes: No collaboration record: four named physicists (Chamberlain, Segrè, Wiegand, Ypsilantis); Lofgren's Bevatron group ran its own experiments in the following weeks (Berkeley Lab History).

No Atlas topic for antimatter exists; topic:precision-and-rare-processes is the nearest, because antiprotons were about one in 50,000 beam particles in 1955. The experiment kind `antimatter` is used as a secondary kind. For the integrator: attach an antimatter topic if one is added.
Berkeley Lab History gives the start of the Segrè-Chamberlain runs as the first week of August 1955 and the first evidence as 21 September 1955; the Physical Review paper is dated 1 November 1955.

physics_goals.locator: Chamberlain Nobel Lecture, section on the design of the experiment
physics_goals.quote: To make this demonstration, it was necessary to show that after the Bevatron beam struck a piece of material, there were present among the particles issuing from nuclear collisions some particles of the same mass as that of the proton, but electrically negative
physics_goals.value: Show that negative particles with the proton mass exist among the products of Bevatron collisions

summary.plain: In August and September 1955 Owen Chamberlain, Emilio Segrè, Clyde Wiegand and Thomas Ypsilantis used Berkeley's new Bevatron to hunt for the proton's antimatter twin. They found negative particles with the proton mass: the antiproton, a prediction of Dirac's theory.
summary.technical: Magnetic-spectrometer and time-of-flight identification of negative particles of proton mass produced when the Bevatron beam struck a target; the Berkeley account says the first evidence came on 21 September 1955, from momentum and velocity, and emulsion stacks confirmed it. Reported in Phys. Rev. 100, 947 (1 November 1955).
